story.lead: COVID-19 has been rising, but positivity has levelled off
story.summary: UKHSA's published figures show COVID-19 climbing in England through late summer and early autumn. The share of tests coming back positive went from **1.7%** in early August to **9.11%** on 19 October. Hospital numbers, which only run to 30 September, rose even faster: about **167** new admissions a day, up from about **13** in mid-July. Here is how the three measures moved.
story.sub: England, UKHSA data dashboard, as published on 26 Oct 2026: test positivity to 19 Oct 2026, hospital figures to 30 Sep 2026.

facts.label: tests positive on 19 Oct 2026, up from 1.7% on 3 Aug
hospital admissions on 30 Sep, up from 12.7 on 15 Jul
beds occupied by COVID patients on 30 Sep

points.h: Positive tests climbed for two months, then paused
points.p: Start with the test results, which are the most recent data. The share of COVID tests that were positive rose every week from **1.7%** on 3 Aug to **9.3%** on 5 Oct. That is more than five times higher. It then stayed at **9.3%** on 12 Oct and edged down to **9.11%** on 19 Oct. So the rise has stopped for now, but one small dip is too little to say it is falling.

points.h: Hospital admissions rose much faster than tests
points.p: Hospitals tell a sharper story, though their figures stop on 30 Sep, three weeks before the test data. The average number of people admitted each day went from **12.7** on 15 Jul to **166.9** on 30 Sep. That is about thirteen times higher. The jump was steepest in September, when it went from **42.3** on 2 Sep to **166.9** on 30 Sep. At that point, admissions were still going up.

points.h: Hospital beds filled up in step
points.p: The number of beds taken by COVID patients followed the same path. It stayed near **140** in July, then reached **930** on 30 Sep. That is about six and a half times the July level. Each week in September added more than the week before, with **673** on 23 Sep and **930** a week later. We can't see beds after 30 Sep, so we can't tell whether hospitals have levelled off like the tests.

story.takeaway: COVID-19 has clearly risen in England since the summer, in tests, admissions and hospital beds. The latest test results suggest the climb may be slowing, with 9.3% twice and then 9.11%. Hospital figures end on 30 Sep, still rising, so they can't yet confirm a turn.
story.note: Hospital admissions here are a count of people per day, not a rate, and every figure is a 7-day rolling average.

story.lead: About 930 COVID patients are in hospital, rising fast
story.summary: UKHSA's published figures show an average of **930** hospital beds in England occupied by COVID-19 patients on 30 September 2026, the latest day available. That is more than **seven times** the **127** recorded in late July (the lowest weekly figure was 126 in mid-June). Yet it is still far below the same date in recent years. The charts below show the recent climb, the comparison with past years, and the year as a whole.

points.h: Numbers have climbed sharply since the summer lull
points.p: Start with the last six months. Hospital COVID patients fell from **321** in early April to a steady level of about 130 to 140 through the summer, with a low of **126** on 17 June. Since early August the numbers have risen every week. They went from **352** on 9 September to **673** a fortnight later, on 23 September and then **930** on 30 September. The last week alone added 257 patients, so the rise is speeding up.

points.h: Even so, it is far lower than in past autumns
points.p: Is this high? Compared with the same date in earlier years, no. On 30 September, **3,439** patients were in hospital in 2023, then **2,681** in 2024 and **1,906** in 2025. This year's **930** is about half of last year's, and roughly a quarter of the 2023 figure. Each year has been lower than the one before on this date.

points.h: Over the year, the autumn peak has long since faded
points.p: Zooming out shows where this rise sits in the past twelve months. October 2025 averaged **2,189** patients, then numbers fell month after month to just **137** in July 2026. The climb since then brought August to **203** and September to **514**. September 2026 is still well below October 2025. The latest figures show a rise from a low base, and they say nothing yet about where it will stop.

story.takeaway: COVID hospital numbers in England are climbing quickly from a very low summer level, reaching 930 on 30 September. They are still much lower than on the same date in each of the last three years. The figures end on that date, so they do not show the most recent weeks.

story.summary: Flu has been climbing in England since July. points.h: Over seven weeks, more tests are coming back positive
points.p: Start with the share of flu tests that find the virus. This is the measure of how common flu is among people who get tested. This year the seven-week average is **4.81%**, against **3.55%** for the same weeks last year. That is a gap of 1.26 percentage points, or roughly a third higher. points.h: Hospital admissions are also higher, by a similar margin

This year's climb has been slower, reaching **6.33%** on 5 October before easing to **5.99%** in the latest week. So the higher average comes from an earlier start, not from a faster rise.

story.takeaway: Flu has been more common this autumn than last at the same point, on both tests and hospital admissions. But last year's rise was steeper, and the latest week is now lower than the same week a year ago. This autumn started earlier, not harder.

story.takeaway: Flu tests began turning positive in early August, hospital admissions rose from late September, and the climb has slowed in the latest weeks. Last year's rise started later but was higher by mid-October.

story.lead: 2022-23 was the worst flu season on record here
story.summary: UKHSA's published figures show that 2022-23 was the heaviest flu season for hospitals in England since the records begin in 2015. At its worst week, **18.09** people per 100,000 were admitted with flu. That is more than double the **7.9** of 2017-18, the highest of the years before it. Below, we look at three ways of measuring a season: hospital admissions, positive tests and intensive care.
story.sub: England, flu seasons from October to May, 2015-16 to 2025-26, as published on 26 Oct 2026. Each season is judged on its single worst week.

points.h: Hospital admissions peaked higher than ever in 2022-23
points.p: Start with the pressure on hospitals. In the worst week of 2022-23, **18.09** people per 100,000 were admitted with flu. The five seasons before the pandemic peaked between 2.58 and 7.9, so this was more than double the highest of them. Two later seasons were also heavy: 2024-25 reached **15.42**, while 2023-24 and 2025-26 peaked at 7.55 and 10.5. Seasons 2020-21 and 2021-22 were very quiet, at 0.05 and 1.15.

points.h: Positive tests tell the same story, with a smaller gap
points.p: Next, how many flu tests came back positive. In the worst week of 2022-23, **32.6%** of tests were positive, about one in three. That is the highest in the series, but the lead is smaller than for admissions. The 2018-19 season reached 28.1% and 2024-25 reached 26.7%. So 2022-23 stood out most in how many people ended up in hospital, rather than in how widely the virus showed up in tests.

points.h: Intensive care admissions were also the highest, but only just
points.p: Finally, the most serious cases. Admissions to intensive care or high-dependency units peaked at **0.64** per 100,000 in 2022-23. That is the highest of the ten seasons shown, but only just ahead of 0.55 in 2017-18 and 0.54 in 2018-19. The 2024-25 season came close at 0.53. For the sickest patients, 2022-23 was among the worst seasons rather than far above the rest.

story.takeaway: On every measure, 2022-23 was the top flu season in England, but by different margins. It was far ahead for hospital admissions, ahead for positive tests, and only narrowly ahead for intensive care. For hospital admissions the 2024-25 season came closest, while 2018-19 was nearest for positive tests and 2017-18 for intensive care.
story.note: Each season is judged on its single worst week, so this shows the height of the peak, not the total over the whole winter.

story.lead: Under-5 RSV admissions peaked highest in winter 2024/25
story.summary: In the busiest week of winter 2024/25, UKHSA's published figures show **47.3** RSV hospital admissions for every 100,000 children under 5. That is the highest winter peak in this data, about **43% higher** than the **33.1** of winter 2022/23. Last winter, 2025/26, came close at **43.8**. Below, we look at the peaks, then the typical week, then the odd summer wave of 2021 that makes the early years hard to compare.
story.sub: UKHSA's published figures for England, RSV hospital admissions in under-5s, October–March winters 2020/21 to 2025/26, as published on 26 Oct 2026.

facts.label: Highest winter peak, 2024/25, under-5s
Peak last winter, 2025/26

points.h: Winter peaks climbed to 47 per 100,000, then eased
points.p: Start with the busiest week of each winter. From 2022/23 to 2024/25 the peak went up each year, from **33.1** to **40.8** to **47.3** admissions per 100,000 under-5s. Last winter's peak was a little lower, at **43.8**, which is 3.5 less than the year before. The two earliest winters are not a fair starting point, and the last chart shows why.

points.h: The typical week tells the same story
points.p: A single peak week can be a fluke, so the next chart averages every week from October to March. It shows the same shape. The average week rose from **10.9** in 2022/23 to **15.0** in 2024/25, then stayed almost level at **14.8** last winter. So the high peaks were not just one freak week: whole winters were busier than in 2022/23. Last winter was very close to the one before.

points.h: Why the first two winters look so different
points.p: Now to the early years. The winter of 2020/21 was almost empty, with a peak of just **0.5**. The next winter, 2021/22, was shaped by something unusual. RSV admissions among under-5s were already high in summer 2021, at **27.9** in August. They then fell month after month to **2.6** by January 2022, more than ten times lower. So the **19.3** peak of 2021/22 was the tail end of a summer wave, not a normal winter one. That is why these two years should not be used as a baseline.

story.takeaway: Since 2022/23, RSV winters among under-5s have been busy, with peaks in the 30s and 40s per 100,000. Winter 2024/25 was the highest in these figures, and last winter was only slightly lower. The first two winters were unlike normal ones, so the clearest comparison starts in 2022/23.
story.note: These are rates per 100,000 children under 5, not numbers of children, and winter means weeks from October to March; weeks from October 2026 onwards (the start of winter 2026/27) are not included.
